analysis.one_liner: Limits how long a ticketing company can hold an exclusive contract to sell a large venue's tickets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large venues often sign one company — like Ticketmaster — as their sole official ticket seller for many years. This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules setting a maximum length for those exclusive contracts, with any contract longer than four years presumed too long. The goal was to open the primary ticketing market to more competition, which supporters argued would lower fees and make it easier for fans to buy tickets.
analysis.who_benefits: Concertgoers, sports fans, and theater audiences who pay the ticketing service fees built into most event tickets. Independent ticketing companies and startups would also gain a fairer chance to win venue contracts, and venues would gain bargaining power when their contracts expire.

how_it_helps.text: Bars primary ticketing providers from signing exclusive contracts with venues of 5,000 or more seats for an 'excessive duration' defined by FTC rules, with a floor of more than four years [S2][S3].
Enforces the ban through the FTC's competition authority, with civil penalties capped at the volume of commerce affected by the violating contract [S3].
Leaves all existing antitrust laws untouched, adding a targeted tool rather than replacing broader enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant primary ticketing companies, whose long exclusive venue contracts are the source of their market power and steady fee revenue. Large venues would give up the guaranteed revenue and advances that come with long exclusive deals.

drawbacks.text: The bill limits only contract length, not exclusivity itself, so a dominant ticketing company could keep renewing exclusive deals just under the FTC-defined limit and hold venues indefinitely [S3].
It exempts venues with fewer than 5,000 seats, leaving smaller clubs and theaters — where service fees are also common — outside the rules [S3].
The ban takes effect only 90 days after FTC rules are finalized, and the bill does not force venues to switch sellers, so real competitive change could take years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to ticket buyers is real but indirect: the bill does not cap fees or guarantee lower prices, it only shortens the length of exclusive contracts so other sellers can compete for venue business. The main costs fall on ticketing companies and venues that profit from long-term exclusivity. A fair-minded reading is that this is a modest, targeted competition measure — it might eventually reduce fees, but it would not fix ticketing problems like bots and scalping on its own.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it, referred it to the Judiciary Committee, and no committee vote or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, with Sen. Richard Blumenthal as the cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant primary ticketing companies keep their long exclusive contracts with large venues unchanged, and the venues that benefit from those guaranteed deals keep them too. Ticket buyers are where they started: still paying the service fees that come with a concentrated ticketing market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant ticketing companies and their venue partners

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Unlock Ticketing Markets Act of 2023 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators acted on the bill (sponsor and one cosponsor); no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Primary ticketing companies (dominated by Ticketmaster/Live Nation)
industries.note: Long exclusive contracts with large venues are the foundation of a dominant ticketing company's market power and its steady service-fee revenue. The bill caps contract length, which would let venues change sellers and give fans alternatives. Its interest in the bill runs directly against ticket buyers, who pay the fees that exclusivity sustains.

Venues would lose the guaranteed revenue, advances, and reduced risk of long exclusive deals, but gain bargaining power and choice among ticket sellers at renewal. Some venue fees may ultimately be passed to fans either way.
Smaller ticket sellers would get periodic openings to compete for large-venue contracts instead of facing decades-long lockups. Their gain comes from competing on price and service for fans.
